rv.q: Her performance triumphantly walks a knife edge between virtuosity and absurdity.
This radical adaptation of Bram Stoker's 1897 vampire classic is a tour de force
Whereas the tongue-in-cheek archness of Williams’s Wilde and Genet treatments felt true to the spirit of their works, it doesn’t quite land here.
This is not just one great performer communing with their crowd.
But I found it almost totally without a sense of any actual horror.
But despite the speed, the atmosphere stays sedate, with none of the fever required, and no peril whatsoever.
It is not her failure that the only performer on stage for an hour and 50 minutes should feel strangely underemployed.
Conceptually it’s an inventive way of communicating this Victorian story, yet the screens also seem to inhibit any real sense of terror.
Goodness knows what this does to her, but for us spectators it is exhausting.
Erivo deserves it, but she also deserves far better – a Dracula with a bit of red meat rather than this bloodless, soul-sapping affair.
Alas, this time it feels effortful rather than fluent – and Erivo seems too stressed to offer more than the odd glimpse of Dracula’s coolly gothic allure.
I wouldn’t go so far as to say it sucks, but it certainly doesn’t bite.
Still, if you arrive at the Noel Coward prepared to marvel at the feat as much as to lose yourself in the tale, you may find the sheer audacity of Erivo’s undertaking is worth the cost of admission.
Yet you feel this is a real example of theatre as an extraordinary feat, a testament to Erivo’s muscular determination, work ethic, and undeniable star power and Williams’ tireless inventiveness.
The show is a mesmerising sight.
Though this adaptation of Dracula certainly doesn’t suck, it is in desperate need of a bit more bite.

The production is a technical feat, but is so caught up in its own cleverness that it forgets one of the most intrinsic appeals of theatre; to connect an actor to an audience through their live presence on stage.
This is, regrettably, one of the worst evenings I have spent in a West End theatre.
Watching TV in the theatre is like visiting a restaurant to read the menu.
